chunks: I was in the presence of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and my father was asking him about the milk from a dead animal, the egg from a dead animal, and the rennet of a dead animal. He said: 'All of this is ritually clean.'

He (al-Husayn) said: So I said to him, 'What about pig hair that is made into a rope and used to draw water from a well from which people drink or perform wudu?' He said: 'There is no problem with it.'
Ali ibn Uqba and Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Ribat added to this, saying: He (the Imam) said, 'And hair and wool — all of it is ritually clean.'
And in the report of Safwan, from al-Husayn ibn Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), he said: 'Hair, wool, fur, feathers, and everything that grows does not become dead (ritually impure).'
He (al-Husayn) said: And I asked him about an egg extracted from the belly of a dead chicken. He said: 'You may eat it.'

key_terms.إِنْفَحَةِ: Rennet (infaha) — the substance found in a young animal's stomach used for coagulating milk in cheese-making
key_terms.الْمَيْتَةِ: Dead animal/carrion (mayta) — an animal that has died without proper Islamic slaughter, whose meat is forbidden
key_terms.ذَكِيٌّ: Ritually clean/pure (dhaki) — here used for items derived from dead animals that are nonetheless considered pure, as opposed to the animal's flesh
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm/problem with it — a standard legal formula indicating permissibility

ai.seo_question: Are eggs, milk, and rennet from dead animals ritually pure in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith records a legal consultation between al-Husayn ibn Zurara, his father Zurara (a senior jurist), and Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) on the ritual purity of products derived from dead animals. The Imam rules that milk, eggs, and rennet from dead animals, as well as pig hair used in ropes for drawing water, are all ritually clean (dhaki). The term 'dhaki' here refers to purity despite the source animal being dead without proper slaughter (mayta). The ruling is significant because it distinguishes between the animal's flesh (impure) and separable non-flesh products (pure), reflecting the Shia jurisprudential principle that things capable of growth and separation are not rendered impure by the death of the host animal.
